The Crest-tailed mulgara (Dasycercus cristicauda) is a medium-sized dasyurid marsupial endemic to the arid and semi-arid regions of central Australia. Field studies indicate that neonatal pups emerge following a gestation period of thirty-eight days [tg = thirty-eight days] at a body temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C], a duration that is relatively short compared to many other small carnivorous marsupials. Newborn offspring are extremely altricial, weighing a mere 0.1 grams [Wwb = 0.1 grams] at the moment of live birth, reflecting the limited energetic reserves available at this early stage of development. This minimal birth mass imposes a substantial reliance on maternal lactation during the subsequent weeks of growth. Daily energetic costs for the mother are consequently high, and the basal metabolic rate for this species has been measured at 36.9 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 36.9 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at the same thermoneutral temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C], a value consistent with predictions for dasyurids of comparable body size.

Suckling juveniles undergo a rapid period of mass gain during the lactation period, remaining entirely dependent on the mother's milk supply. The weaning process, marked by a dietary transition from milk to solid food, typically concludes at one hundred and twenty-one days [tx = one hundred and twenty-one days] since birth at 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C]. At this critical juncture, weaned juveniles achieve a wet weight of approximately 22 grams [Wwx = approximately 22 grams], having more than doubled their size compared to the neonatal stage. This mass remains modest relative to adults, however, as the growth trajectory continues steadily through the sub-adult phase. Nutritional emancipation from the mother allows these young individuals to begin foraging independently, though they must navigate the challenges of a harsh, unpredictable environment. Mortality during this period is thought to be substantial, driven by both predation and resource limitation in the arid interior where prey availability fluctuates dramatically with seasonal rainfall.

Sexual maturation in the Crest-tailed mulgara represents a significant developmental milestone that occurs relatively late in the first year of life. Puberty is reached at three hundred and fifteen days [tp = three hundred and fifteen days] since birth at 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C], a delay that likely reflects the time needed to attain the necessary body condition for successful reproduction in a resource-poor habitat. Upon reaching this adult stage, females achieve an ultimate wet weight of 120 grams [Wwi = 120 grams], whereas males are considerably larger, with an ultimate wet weight of 185 grams [Wwi = 185 grams]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in body mass is characteristic of many dasyurids and is often linked to intrasexual competition among males for access to breeding females. The 65-gram difference between sexes suggests a polygynous or promiscuous mating system, corroborated by field observations of male-biased dispersal and larger home ranges.

At the thermoneutral temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C], reproductive output in this species is highly constrained by the aridity of its environment. Females typically produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], with a litter size of seven pups [N_R_i = a litter size of seven pups], representing a modest annual reproductive rate. The maximum longevity documented for the Crest-tailed mulgara in the wild is approximately 2,701 days [am = approximately 2,701 days], translating to about 7.4 years of potential life at a temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C]. This lifespan, combined with the single annual litter, indicates a relatively slow life-history pace for a mammal of this body size. The trade-off between current reproduction and survival is evident here, as the energetic demands of gestation and lactation are substantial. Under favorable conditions, females are capable of breeding every year, but extended droughts frequently result in skipped reproductive seasons, adding a layer of demographic variability.

Comparative physiological studies situate the Crest-tailed mulgara within the broader spectrum of desert-adapted dasyurids. The same thermoneutral temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C] that characterizes its resting metabolic rate also defines the developmental context for its life-history events, a pattern observed in other desert dasyurids where thermal conditions synchronize reproductive and metabolic schedules. The 38-day gestation period (38 days) [tg = 38 days] is notably shorter than that of the larger fat-tailed dunnart, yet longer than in some smaller planigales, suggesting that within dasyurids, gestation length scales positively with body mass but may be further modulated by the unpredictability of resource pulses in arid systems at a temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C]. Ecological observations from long-term trapping programs in the Simpson Desert indicate that the species is capable of surviving multiple consecutive drought years, a resilience partially attributable to its relatively low basal oxygen consumption of 36.9 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 36.9 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C]. This reduced metabolic demand likely facilitates persistence during periods when prey such as beetles, spiders, and small reptiles become scarce, allowing the mulgara to maintain body condition better than sympatric competitors with higher energetic requirements.
